questions.question: A boy wonders whether the length of a paper plane's wings changes how far it glides. Before he folds a single plane, he writes in his notebook: "If a paper plane has longer wings, then it will glide farther." What has he written?
choices: A hypothesis
A theory
A law
A model
questions.context: A hypothesis is a testable idea about what will happen, often written as "if..., then...", and folding planes with short and long wings and measuring their glides will test it. A law or a theory rests on a great many tests already done, and a model is a copy or picture of something, such as a globe.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.1H asks 6th graders to tell hypotheses, theories and laws apart, and 6th-grade investigations open by stating a testable hypothesis, usually in if-then form.

questions.question: A man says that a fire-breathing dragon lives in his garage. His friend sees nothing there, but the dragon is invisible, the man explains. Flour on the floor would show no footprints, since the dragon floats, and a heat camera would find nothing, since its fire gives off no heat. Why is his claim not a scientific hypothesis?
questions.answer: No test could ever show it to be wrong
choices: No test could ever show it to be wrong
No scientist has proven it to be true
It is not written as an if-then sentence
It is about a dragon, a creature of old stories
questions.context: A scientific hypothesis must be testable: some observation has to be able to tell whether it is right. Every test the friend can think of meets a new excuse, so no evidence could ever count against the dragon; a dragon that left footprints in the flour would be a claim science could check. The astronomer Carl Sagan told this tale in The Demon-Haunted World and asked how such a dragon differs from no dragon at all.
questions.grade_note: Judging whether an idea is testable is part of telling a scientific hypothesis apart (TEKS 6.1H), and NGSS 6-8 teaches that science limits itself to what observation and evidence can reach.

questions.question: A scientist's hypothesis says that a small meat-eating dinosaur was covered in feathers. No dinosaur of its kind has been alive for millions of years, and no one has ever seen one. Can her hypothesis be tested?
questions.answer: Yes, by searching its fossils for traces of feathers
choices: Yes, by searching its fossils for traces of feathers
Yes, by asking other scientists whether it had feathers
No, for no one has ever seen one alive
No, for ideas about the past cannot be tested
questions.context: Ideas about the past are tested by what the past left behind. Fossils in fine-grained rock in China have kept the feathers of small meat-eating dinosaurs: Sinosauropteryx, described in 1996, was the first, and over 30 feathered kinds are now known. Asking other scientists is no test: however many of them agree, only the rocks can show whether it had feathers.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that scientists test ideas by careful observation as well as by experiment (TEKS 6.1B's descriptive investigations; NGSS 6-8), so an idea about the past can still be a testable hypothesis.

questions.question: Ravi's hypothesis says that a can of water painted black warms up faster in sunshine than one painted white. He tests ten pairs of cans on five sunny days, and every time the black can warms faster. What can he now say about his hypothesis?
choices: His results support it
His results prove it true for good
His results tell nothing about it yet
His results count for nothing until he knows why
questions.context: Results that agree with a hypothesis support it, even before anyone can explain why it holds. Science does not call an idea proven for good, since a later test under other conditions could still find a case where it fails, so scientists keep testing even well-supported ideas.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade TEKS describe a hypothesis as an idea that evidence supports or does not support, and middle-school lessons teach the word supported, not proven.

questions.question: Told to wash his hands before dinner, a boy shrugs. Germ theory, the idea that many illnesses are caused by germs too small to see, is only a theory, he says, and a theory is just a guess. What does "theory" mean to a scientist?
questions.answer: A well-tested explanation of how nature works
choices: A well-tested explanation of how nature works
A guess that is still waiting for its first test
An idea one step short of becoming a law
A rule that has been proven true forever
questions.context: In everyday speech a theory can be a hunch, but to a scientist it is an explanation backed by a large body of evidence from many tests over many years. Germ theory has more than a century of such evidence behind it, from the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch onward. A theory does not turn into a law, and science calls no idea proven forever.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade curriculum line says outright that 'theory' in science does not mean a guess (TEKS 6.1H; NGSS 6-8 on the word's everyday use).

questions.question: Students hang weights from a spring and measure how far it stretches. Every extra weight they add stretches it by the same extra amount. Scientists have found this steady pattern in spring after spring, as long as none is overstretched, and they sum it up in one short statement, often written as an equation. What kind of statement is it?
choices: A law
A theory
A hypothesis
An observation
questions.context: A law sums up a pattern found again and again, often as an equation; this one is Hooke's law, named after Robert Hooke, who stated it in the 1670s. It says how far a spring stretches, not why, and it fails once a spring is stretched past its limit. An observation is one thing seen, a hypothesis is an idea still to be tested, and a theory explains why something happens.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.1H and NGSS 6-8 teach that a law is a regular pattern in nature, often described mathematically, and 6th graders meet springs stretching under weights in their force labs.

questions.question: Isaac Newton's law of gravity, published in 1687, applies to every pair of masses, from an apple and Earth to the Sun and its planets. Yet in a later edition of his book, Newton wrote that one thing about gravity was still beyond him. What did his law leave unexplained?
questions.answer: What causes the pull of gravity
choices: What causes the pull of gravity
How strongly two masses pull each other
How the pull weakens with distance
Which way the pull of gravity acts
questions.context: A law describes what happens, here how strongly two masses pull on each other and how the pull weakens with distance, without saying why. Newton wrote that he had not been able to discover the cause of gravity's properties, and he refused to make up a guess. More than two centuries later, Albert Einstein's general relativity, a theory, explained gravity as mass bending space and time.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade curriculum line names Newton's laws as its example of laws, and the lesson teaches that a law describes a pattern without explaining it.

questions.question: When a sealed-in gas is squeezed into half the space at the same temperature, its pressure doubles. Scientists found this pattern in the 1600s and call it a law. The particle theory of gases accounts for it: crowded closer, the gas's moving particles strike the walls more often. Will the theory one day become a law?
questions.answer: No, for the two do different jobs
choices: No, for the two do different jobs
Yes, once it has been tested enough
Yes, once it is written as an equation
No, for only a law can be written as an equation
questions.context: A law describes a pattern and a theory explains why it happens, so neither grows into the other. The gas law, Boyle's law, goes back to Robert Boyle's measurements of 1662, and the particle theory is still a theory after more than 150 years of tests. The theory even has equations of its own.
questions.grade_note: Telling a theory from a law is TEKS 6.1H, and 6th graders already know the particle model of gases, which gives them a theory and a law about the same thing.

questions.question: Mia tells her class that Newton's laws of motion deserve more trust than cell theory, because a law has been proven and a theory has not. Is she right?
questions.answer: No, both rest on a great deal of evidence
choices: No, both rest on a great deal of evidence
Yes, a law has been proven true for good
Yes, a law has been tested more times than any theory
No, a theory always deserves more trust than a law
questions.context: Laws and theories do different jobs, and both are among the best-tested knowledge in science: Newton's laws describe how forces change motion, and cell theory explains how living things are built. Neither is proven forever; Newton's laws, for one, give way to Einstein's relativity at speeds close to the speed of light.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade line names both cell theory and Newton's laws, and the lesson teaches that theories and laws are both strong and neither outranks the other.

969c0badad.why: Judge (medium tell): 'Only one person has ever believed it' was dead. It is replaced by the judge's lure, 'It is about a dragon, a creature of old stories', for the student who judges a claim by its subject and not by whether it can be tested (F6). Judge (low): the two old-fashioned 'for' clauses now read 'since'. Key unchanged; the context now says that the subject does not decide it.

95026a0345.why: Judge (medium tell): the model lure was weak, leaving the fossil key as plain common sense. It is replaced by the judge's misconception that agreement tests an idea (F29: Berkeley, ideas are judged by evidence, not popularity), worded to share the stem's 'feathers' so the key is not the only choice that echoes it. The judge's 'no experiment' lure was not used: it would stand or fall with 'ideas about the past cannot be tested', the M4 lure already here. Stem and key unchanged.

caeaf20e1e.why: Judge (medium tell): all three lures were absolute overclaims and two stood or fell together, so the modest key fell to elimination. Judge and fact-check (medium): the law lure and the context's 'a few weeks of one student's tests do not make a law' implied that a hypothesis becomes a law after enough tests, the promotion ladder the unit rejects (M2). The law lure and that clause are gone; no choice now says a hypothesis turns into anything. The new lures are the judge's modest-sounding wrong ones (results tell nothing yet; they count for nothing until he knows why). Stem and key unchanged.

619daa9136.why: Fact-check (error): 'has been a law since Robert Boyle measured it in 1662' is untrue; Boyle never stated the relation as a law, and his 1662 table calls it 'the hypothesis' (F28). The context now says Boyle's law goes back to Boyle's measurements of 1662. Judge (low, cheap fix): the weak lure 'a theory can never be tested' is replaced by 'only a law can be written as an equation', which the context answers (the theory has equations of its own). Stem and key unchanged.

5aa6ca9275.why: Judge (medium clarity): for this pair, 'a theory deserves more trust than a law' could be defended, since Newton's laws give way near the speed of light. The lure is now general, 'a theory always deserves more trust than a law', as the judge proposed. Judge (low): 'a theory is still partly a guess' re-tested the theory-meaning question's key; it is replaced by the judge's 'a law has been tested more times than any theory', another wrong ranking (F27). Stem and key unchanged.
